understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call not feeling good enough, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: By the end of the week the thought that nothing matters is named, and the part of you that asks is held as real and not ending.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the weight of the thought and the numbness, named without judgment.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that it is a state of mind, not the truth of who you are.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the self that asks is not the self that ends.
week_beats.act: You try one act of staying with someone you trust and not acting on the thought.
week_beats.story: A young seeker who felt the world was empty shows you that what is real in you cannot end.

understanding.core_struggle: A student under twenty-five says they do not want to be here anymore and thinks about ending it, finding nothing meaningful.
understanding.mirror: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.
understanding.insight: What you're carrying is heavy, and it is not a measure of your worth. You don't have to carry it alone.

queries.hook: When the darkness feels endless and the heart is too tired to go on, and no one seems to see the pain.
queries.diagnose: When the mind turns against itself, it says nothing matters and that life should end; this is a state of mind, not the truth of who you are.
queries.steady: This darkness is a passing night, not the whole of you; the self within you is whole, held and never alone.
queries.act: Hold on through the dark night and reach out to someone who cares; the self within you is not broken and is never alone.
queries.story: A young seeker who felt the world was empty and the self was small, who found the truth that is not born and does not die.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी । यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥
verse.line: What the crowd sleeps through, the wise stay awake to. What the crowd chases, the wise see past.
verse.translation: What is night for all beings, in that the self-controlled one is awake; and where all beings are awake, that is night for the seeing sage.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna's question about what a person of steady mind looks like. He describes someone who is awake when the crowd sleeps, and who sees past the things the crowd chases. He explains that steadiness is built by guarding attention. Anger and ruin start when you dwell on the wrong things.
verse.for_you: You feel numb because your mind has been awake to the noise of the crowd, the endless scroll and the heavy thoughts, while the rest of the world seems to be sleeping. Nothing feels meaningful because your attention has been caught in a loop.
verse.try_today: Put the phone down for one minute and look at the wall, then the window, then your own hands.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own restless night, and the crowd is fast asleep.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to stay steady when people and wealth come and go.
verse.sanskrit: मानसानां पुनर्योनिर्दुःखानां चित्तविभ्रमः / अनिष्टोपनिपातो वा तृतीयं नोपपद्यते
verse.line: Mental pain comes from two places: something you didn't want happened, or your mind is spinning. No third.
verse.translation: Sorrow of the mind has only two sources: a confused, wandering mind, or something unwanted happening to you. There is no third.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: King Janaka once asked the sage Ashma how a person stays steady when wealth and people come and go. Ashma said sorrow of the mind has only two sources. The first is something unwanted happening to you, like a friend leaving or a plan falling apart. The second is your own mind spinning in circles, unable to settle on one thing. There is no third source for mental pain. This means the numbness you feel is not a verdict on your life.
verse.for_you: You sit with six hours on your phone because your mind is spinning. It is not that your life is empty. It is that your mind cannot settle on one thing long enough to feel it. This numbness is a state of mind, not the truth of who you are.
verse.try_today: Name the two things spinning in your mind right now.
verse.scene_line: You are the king asking the sage how to stay steady when nothing stays.

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Yama on the inner self and the world's pain.
verse.sanskrit: सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः । एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ॥
verse.line: The sun shows every flaw yet stays untouched. Your deepest self stays untouched by the world's sorrow.
verse.translation: Just as the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the flaws the eyes see outside, so the one inner self of all beings is not stained by the sorrow of the world; it stands apart.
verse.why: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

prasang.title: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

verse.meaning: Yama is speaking to Nachiketa, a young seeker who has come to the edge of death itself to learn what lasts. He speaks of the sun, the one thing that sees everything yet is never stained by the dirt it looks upon. He says the same is true for the deepest self inside you. The sorrow and flaws of the world touch the surface, but they cannot touch what is at your core. What the verse proposes is a turning inward. The pain you feel is real, but it is not the whole of you.
verse.for_you: Your mind is restless, and nothing feels meaningful right now. That numbness is a heavy weight. But the part of you that feels this emptiness, that notices the six hours on your phone, that is not a flaw. It is the part that asks, and it is still here.
verse.try_today: Put the phone down and look at one thing in the room without judging it.
verse.scene_line: You are Nachiketa, standing at the door of the self that cannot be stained.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how to be free. Ashtavakra answers that the whole world is strung on you and pervaded by you. You are pure awareness by nature, so do not let your mind shrink into pettiness or smallness.
verse.for_you: The numbness you feel is not the whole of you. That part of you which asks why nothing matters is still awake. It is not a flaw that needs fixing but a witness that is holding on. Let it hold.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment where the numbness lifts and something feels slightly less heavy.
verse.scene_line: You are the awareness in which the exam room and the phone screen both appear.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The seer speaks to you directly. They tell you to do your work. They say you may wish to live a full hundred years. The point is that you could act, but let your actions go. When you do your part and let it go, the action does not stick to you. It is a way to live fully without being trapped by what you do.
verse.for_you: You sit with the weight of not feeling good enough, and the phone is a way to numb that. The seer is not saying the weight is false. They are saying you can do your part and still let it go.
verse.try_today: Sit with the feeling for five minutes without picking up the phone.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own study, the screen is dark, and the work is still there.

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: पापं चेत्पुरुषः कृत्वा कल्याणमभिपद्यते / मुच्यते सर्वपापेभ्यो महाभ्रेणेव चन्द्रमाः
verse.line: Turn to doing good after a wrong, and you come out like the moon from behind a cloud.
verse.translation: If a person who has done wrong turns to doing good, he is freed from all his wrongs, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: In Mithila, a Brahmin ascetic named Kaushika is sent to learn from a meat-seller named Dharmavyadha. The ascetic expects wisdom in a cave or forest, but the butcher teaches him that goodness lives in ordinary work done honestly. The butcher tells him that if a person turns to doing good after a wrong, they are freed from it, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud.
verse.for_you: You are in your own Mithila, looking for meaning in a place you did not expect. The numbness you feel is not a sign that you are broken. It is the weight of carrying too much alone.
verse.try_today: Tell one person you trust what you are feeling right now.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own shop, waiting to be taught by a voice you did not expect.

story.title: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
story.story_hook: The prince who had everything came back from his travels and stopped laughing.
story.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
story.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

anchor.setting: Rama's attendants tell King Dasharatha how the prince has changed since his pilgrimage.

anchor.line: Ever since he came back from the trip, he hasn't been himself.
anchor.translation: Ever since lotus-eyed Rama came back from his pilgrimage with the brahmins, he has been low in spirit.
anchor.why: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

story.for_you: You sit with the phone and the screen, and nothing pulls you in. That numbness you feel is not a failure of your mind, it is a signal that your questions need air. Rama did not get better by forcing himself to care.
